info.name: IZSuite - API
info.description:
Every endpoint the izSuite Nuxt frontend talks to: user authentication plus the public read-only lists.

**Base URL**
IIS holds port 80 on this machine, so Laragon nginx serves the vhost on port **8080**. The `:8080` is required - without it the request hits IIS and comes back as a 404 HTML page.

- Laragon vhost: `http://izsuite-admin.test:8080/api/v1` (default)
- artisan serve: `http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/v1`

---

## Auth

Sanctum personal access tokens, not session cookies. `POST /auth/login` returns a plain-text token; send it back as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.

**Run "Login" first.** Its test script writes the token into the `token` variable, and the two requests that need it (`Me`, `Logout`) read it from there, so they just work afterwards.

Token lifetime is driven by `remember`:
- `remember: true` -> 30 days
- `remember: false` or absent -> 12 hours

**Two ways to sign out**

| Endpoint | Revokes | Response |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /auth/logout` | Only the token that made the request - other devices stay signed in | `{ message }` |
| `POST /auth/logout-all` | Every token the user holds, this one included | `{ message, revoked_tokens }` |

Both are token-level. Neither touches the **admin panel** session at `/login` - that is separate, cookie-based auth on the `web` guard, and it signs out via `POST /logout`.

**Credentials go in the body, never the URL.** `POST /auth/login?email=..&password=..` is refused with 400 even when the values are correct, because a query string is recorded in access logs, browser history and `Referer` headers.

`device_name` is optional and only labels the token, so a user can tell their sessions apart in a future "active devices" screen.

**Re-running the whole collection**
One full run makes 9 login attempts and 5 register attempts. Both endpoints allow 10 per minute per IP, so there is almost no headroom on login. A second run started inside the same minute fails with 429s, and so will the first run if you have been clicking Send by hand. Wait a minute, or clear the counters:

```
php artisan cache:clear
```

**Registering**
`POST /auth/register` takes the fields the frontend's Owner information form collects and returns the same token/user shape as login, so a new account is signed in immediately. New accounts get the `user` role.

The Register body is sent verbatim - type your own values and those are saved. Because `username` and `email` are unique, **re-sending Register unchanged returns 422**; change them to create another account. The four `Register - ...` failure requests are safe to re-send as often as you like.

Email verification is **not** part of this yet: there is no verify endpoint, so registration marks the address verified rather than leaving every new account unable to log in. When the verification flow ships, that one line in AuthService::register() comes out.

**Who may sign in here**
Frontend users only, and only fully set-up ones. Three separate 403s:

| Condition | Message | `action` |
|---|---|---|
| Admin, staff or super-admin role | Sign in through the admin panel at `/login` | - |
| `status` is not `active` | Account is not active, contact support | - |
| `email_verified_at` is null | Verify your email first | `verification_required` |

The password is always checked first, so all three are only reachable by someone who already knows the credentials - the endpoint never reveals *why* an account it does not own would be refused.

Seeded accounts for these: `admin@izsuite.io` (admin) and `unverified@izsuite.io` (unverified).

**Seeded demo account**
`user@izsuite.io` / `123456`. If it is missing, run `php artisan db:seed --class=RoleSeeder` then `php artisan db:seed --class=UserSeeder`.

**Login response**
```json
{
  "message": "Signed in successfully.",
  "token": "1|xxxxxxxx",
  "token_type": "Bearer",
  "expires_at": "2026-10-09T14:43:16+00:00",
  "user": {
    "id": 10,
    "name": "izSuite User",
    "email": "user@izsuite.io",
    "phone": null,
    "headline": null,
    "bio": null,
    "avatar_url": null,
    "role": { "id": 105, "name": "User", "slug": "user" },
    "status": "active",
    "timezone": "UTC",
    "currency": "USD",
    "is_email_verified": true,
    "email_verified_at": "2026-09-09T14:42:51+00:00",
    "last_login_at": "2026-09-09T14:43:16+00:00",
    "created_at": "2026-09-09T14:42:52+00:00"
  }
}
```

---

## Public lists

App categories, apps and plans. No token required.

```json
{
  "data": [ ... ],
  "pagination": {
    "current_page": 1,
    "last_page": 1,
    "per_page": 15,
    "total": 3,
    "from": 1,
    "to": 3,
    "has_prev_page": false,
    "has_next_page": false
  }
}
```

---

## Status codes

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 200 | OK |
| 201 | Contact message created |
| 400 | Credentials were sent in the query string instead of the body |
| 401 | Credentials do not match, or token missing, expired or revoked |
| 403 | Admin account, inactive account, or unverified email |
| 422 | Request body or query string failed validation |
| 429 | More than 10 login attempts from one IP in a minute |

Failures answer with `{ "message": "..." }`; validation failures add an `errors` object keyed by field name.

Run them top to bottom - Login stores the token that Me and Logout consume.

request.description:
Creates a frontend account and emails it a 6-digit activation code. **No token comes back** - the account cannot sign in until the code is verified, so the next screen is the OTP box rather than the app.

**The body is sent exactly as written.** Nothing rewrites it, so put in whatever values you want and those are what get saved.

`username` and `email` are unique, so sending the same ones twice returns **422 - already taken**. To register again, change them.

| Field | Required | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `first_name` | **yes** | Saved verbatim |
| `last_name` | no | Saved verbatim |
| `username` | **yes** | Unique, 3-30 chars, starts with a letter or digit, then letters/digits/`.`/`_`/`-`. Stored lower-cased |
| `email` | **yes** | Unique. Stored lower-cased |
| `password` | **yes** | Min 8, with upper and lower case, a number and a symbol |
| `password_confirmation` | **yes** | Must match `password` |
| `accept_terms` | **yes** | Must be true |

The new account gets the `user` role, `status: active`, `terms_accepted_at` set to now, and `email_verified_at` **null**.

request.description:
Revokes **only** the token that made this request. Re-running `Me` afterwards returns 401, but the user's other sessions keep working - the test here proves it against `{{second_device_token}}`.

This is what a normal "Sign out" button calls. For "sign out everywhere", see `Logout everywhere` below.

request.description:
Revokes **every** token the user holds, the one making this request included, and answers with the count:

```json
{ "message": "Signed out of all devices.", "revoked_tokens": 2 }
```

This is what a "sign out everywhere" button calls - a lost phone, a shared computer, or after a password change.

The test checks `{{second_device_token}}` is now 401, which is exactly the assertion `Logout` makes in reverse.

// after the response, by which time the password would already have
// been changed. skipRequest is the only thing that gets in front of it.
console.log('Change password skipped - set run_password_change to 1 to really change it.');
pm.test("other devices are signed out, this one is not", function () {
pm.test("neither password is echoed back", function () {
// Only on success, and only in Postman: a runner cannot write the
// new value back to the file, so leaving it set after a failure
// would point every later sign-in at a password that was never set.

request.description:
The "I know my password and want a different one" case; the reset folder is for people who do not.

**Validation is identical to the admin profile form** - the same `current_password` check and the same `Password::defaults()` policy - so the API is not a weaker way in.

Every **other** session is signed out and `revoked_tokens` says how many; the token that made the request keeps working, since signing this device out would only make you log straight back in.

**Off by default.** This really changes the password on `{{user_email}}`, and a runner cannot write the new value back into the collection file - so an unattended run would change the fixture and then fail to sign in on the next pass. Set `run_password_change` to `1` when you want to exercise it, and update `user_password` afterwards.

The two 422 cases above run unattended: they are rejected before anything is written.

query.description: Rejected: credentials may not travel in a URL.
Rejected: credentials may not travel in a URL.

request.description:
Correct credentials, but in the query string instead of the body - refused with 400.

Laravel's `input()` reads the query string as well as the body, so without an explicit guard this would sign you in. A URL is not a private channel: it is written verbatim into web-server access logs, browser history, bookmarks and outgoing `Referer` headers, so a password sent this way ends up on disk in several places.

The guard fires on the parameter *name*, so even `?email&password` with empty values is refused - the point is to make a client that gets this wrong fail loudly rather than leak quietly.

item.name: Email verification
item.description:
The step between registering and signing in. Register emails a 6-digit code; this folder spends it.

**The happy-path request needs a human.** The code only exists in the inbox, so no runner can read it: register, open the email, paste the digits into the `verify_otp` collection variable, then send **Verify email**. Until that variable is filled the request reports itself as skipped, so a full run stays green.

Every failure case below runs unattended.

A failed verify returns 422 with `errors.otp` and a top-level `action`:

| `action` | Means |
|---|---|
| `code_invalid` | Wrong digits, no code on file, or an address with no account |
| `code_expired` | Right digits, but past the 30 minute expiry |

Branch on `action`, never on the wording - the sentences are free to change and to be translated.

exec: pm.test("carries action code_invalid and errors.otp", function () {

request.description: Six zeros against a real pending code. Also what an unknown address returns - the two are deliberately identical, so the endpoint cannot be used to find out who has an account.

exec: pm.test("rejected on length, before any lookup", function () {

request.description: Caught by validation before the code is looked up at all, so there is no `action` on this one - it is an ordinary 422.

exec: pm.test("skipped - paste the emailed code into the verify_otp variable", function () {

request.description:
Spends the code and activates the account. Pasted spaces and dashes are stripped, so the digits can be copied straight out of the email.

Afterwards the code is cleared - sending it again returns the idempotent "already verified" success, not a second activation.

Run **Login** next: it succeeds from here on.

exec: // A second run inside 60 seconds is answered by the cooldown, not the
// happy path - both are correct, so assert whichever arrived.
pm.test("cooldown says how long to wait", function () {
// An account that is already active is answered, correctly, with no code.
pm.test("already active accounts are told so, and no code is sent", function () {
// Assert the fields, not the sentence: the wording is free to change and
// to be translated, and a test that pins it would break on both.
pm.test("a code went to the address that was asked for", function () {

request.description:
Re-issues a code.

| Answer | When |
|---|---|
| **200** `A new code is on its way` | Unverified account, outside the cooldown |
| **200** `action: already_verified` | The account is active already - not an error, and no mail is sent |
| **429** `action: cooldown_active` | A code went out under 60 seconds ago; `retry_after_seconds` says how long is left |
| **422** `action: account_not_found` | No account on that address |

item.name: Password reset
item.description:
Forgot password in three steps.

| Step | Endpoint | Buys |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `POST /auth/password/forgot` | A 6-digit code, emailed |
| 2 | `POST /auth/password/verify-code` | A single-use `reset_token`, valid 15 minutes |
| 3 | `POST /auth/password/reset` | The new password |

Step 2 is what stops step 3 being called on its own: without a token issued by it there is nothing to spend. Both the code and the token are single use, and both are stored hashed.

**To run the happy path:** send **Forgot password**, open the email, paste the digits into `reset_otp`, send **Verify code** - it saves `reset_token` for you - then send **Reset password**. The steps that need the emailed code report themselves as skipped until you fill the variable, so a full run stays green.

Failure `action` codes: `code_invalid`, `code_expired`, `reset_token_invalid`.

Resetting revokes every session on the account and changes the **password only**. Email verification is registration's business: nothing here sets that flag or reads it, and login runs its own checks when the account next signs in.

exec: // A second run inside 60 seconds is answered by the cooldown, not the
// happy path - both are correct, so assert whichever arrived.
pm.test("cooldown says how long to wait", function () {
// Assert the fields, not the sentence: the wording is free to change and
// to be translated, and a test that pins it would break on both.
pm.test("a code went to the address that was asked for", function () {

request.description:
Step 1. Emails a 6-digit code, valid 30 minutes.

An address with no account here is refused outright - **422** with `action: account_not_found`. An **admin** address gets that same answer: admins sign in through the session-based panel, and a public endpoint that reset an admin password would hand the panel a door it never asked for. Reusing the not-found wording keeps this from being a way to pick admin accounts out of a list.

Asking again inside 60 seconds returns **429** with `action: cooldown_active` and the seconds left.

Now open the email and paste the digits into the `reset_otp` variable.

exec: pm.test("says plainly that there is no such account", function () {

request.description:
An address with no account is told so, rather than given a vague "if it exists" reply.

That does let a caller work out which addresses are registered. It was weighed and accepted: **register already answers the same question** - a signup form has to say "this email is taken" - so staying vague here bought very little while leaving a real user unable to tell a typo from a mail that never arrived.

**An admin address returns this byte for byte.** Admin roles are excluded from the `exists` check rather than refused further in, so an admin address and an unregistered one are indistinguishable - otherwise this would be a way to pick the admin accounts out of a list.

It is an ordinary validation failure, so there is no `action` on it: read `errors.email` the way you read any other field error.

exec: pm.test("carries action code_invalid and errors.otp", function () {

request.description: Digits are checked before expiry on purpose. Expiry first would answer "is there a stale code for this address?" to anyone typing six zeros - so only someone who typed the real code, meaning someone holding the email, is ever told that it expired.

pm.test("hands back a single-use reset token", function () {
// Step three needs it, so hand it straight to the next request.

request.description:
Step 2. Spends the code and returns a `reset_token` - 64 random characters, stored hashed, good for 15 minutes and one use.

The code is retired the moment it buys a token, so sending it twice returns `code_invalid`.

The test saves `reset_token` into the collection variables, so **Reset password** is ready to send.

exec: pm.test("carries action reset_token_invalid and errors.reset_token", function () {

request.description: A made-up token. The same answer covers an expired token and one that has already been spent - there is nothing useful to tell apart.

exec: pm.test("the password policy is checked before the token", function () {

request.description:
A reset is not a way in under a weaker rule: the same `Password::defaults()` policy applies here as on registration, the staff forms and the admin profile - min 8, upper and lower case, a number and a symbol.

The token is deliberately nonsense to show that validation runs first: the failure is about the password, not the token.

exec: pm.test("skipped - run Verify code first - it fills reset_token", function () {
pm.test("the new password is never echoed back", function () {
// Spent. Leaving it set would make the next run look like it worked.
// Sign in with it from now on.

request.description:
Step 3. Sets the password and revokes every session on the account - a reset is what someone does when they think the account is not theirs alone any more, so leaving the other devices signed in would defeat the point.

**The password is all that changes.** Email verification belongs to registration; this endpoint neither sets that flag nor reads it. An account that never confirmed its address is still refused by **Login**, which answers for itself with `action: verification_required` - send it to **Resend verification code** from there.

The token is spent here. Sending it again returns `reset_token_invalid`.
